blocks.text:
Design the core message routing engine behind a publish-subscribe system (the kind that powers Kafka topics or Google Cloud Pub/Sub). Two mechanics separate this from a plain direct-callback observer: wildcard topic matching, where a subscriber can subscribe to a pattern like "orders.*" and receive every message published under that family of topics, and acknowledgment-based delivery, where a message sits in a subscriber's own queue until explicitly acknowledged, gets redelivered if it times out, and is moved to a dead-letter list after too many failed attempts.

  • Actors: Publisher (publishes messages), Subscriber (subscribes to topic patterns and processes messages), PubSubService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: exact and wildcard topic matching, per-subscriber message queues, acknowledgment, timeout-based redelivery, and dead-lettering.

The distinguishing mechanic is durable, acknowledged delivery: unlike a direct observer callback that fires once and forgets, a message here lives in a subscriber's queue until explicitly acknowledged, and an unacknowledged message is redelivered up to a fixed number of times before being set aside in a dead-letter list.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Subscribe to a topic pattern: an exact topic name, or a wildcard pattern using a single-segment wildcard.
Publish a message: route one copy to every subscriber with at least one matching subscription.
Receive a message: a subscriber pulls the next pending message from its own queue, marking it in flight.
Acknowledge a message: confirm successful processing, removing it from in-flight tracking.
Redeliver or dead-letter: a message left unacknowledged past a timeout is redelivered up to a retry limit, then moved to a dead-letter list.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting many topics, subscribers, and in-flight messages must not require touching existing routing logic.
Extensibility: a new matching rule (multi-level wildcards, regular expressions) should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: matching, notification, and id creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: routing a published message is proportional to the number of registered subscriptions.
Thread safety: two concurrent receive calls on the same subscriber must never both dequeue the exact same message.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Should wildcards support multiple levels (matching a variable number of segments), or only a single segment at a time?
Should message ordering be strictly preserved per subscriber, even across redeliveries?
Is there a maximum queue size per subscriber, and what happens when it is exceeded?
Should a subscriber be able to unsubscribe from a pattern, and how should in-flight messages for that pattern be handled?
Is exactly-once delivery required, or is at-least-once, with the possibility of duplicate processing, acceptable?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: Wildcard patterns support a single-segment wildcard only, a pattern and a topic must have the same number of dot-separated segments to ever match.
Delivery is at-least-once, a redelivered message may in principle be processed more than once by the same subscriber.
Timeouts are modeled as an explicit tick counter advanced by the caller, rather than real wall-clock time, to keep behavior deterministic and testable.
Subscriber queues are unbounded in this design, a maximum queue size and its overflow behavior are noted as a follow-up.
A message is delivered to a subscriber at most once per publish call, even if more than one of that subscriber's patterns matches the topic.

blocks.text: The design centers on three core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: Message, Subscriber, and Subscription

items: Message: one published event, its topic, payload, and how many times it has been delivered.
Subscriber: one consumer, with its own pending queue, in-flight tracking, and dead-letter list.
Subscription: one topic pattern a subscriber has registered interest in.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A publisher publishes messages; a subscriber holds many subscriptions; a message is routed to every matching subscriber, who queues it until acknowledged or dead lettered

items: Subscriber to Subscription is one-to-many.
Message to Subscriber is many-to-many at the routing level, but each subscriber tracks its own independent copy and lifecycle for a delivered message.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep topic matching, notification, and id creation decoupled from the core service.
Why needed: an exact subscription and a wildcard subscription fundamentally disagree on how to compare a pattern against a topic, and that decision genuinely varies per subscription.

metadata.alt: TopicMatchingStrategy interface with ExactTopicMatchingStrategy and WildcardTopicMatchingStrategy implementations

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: a future multi-level wildcard or regular-expression matching rule is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to the core routing logic in PubSubService. What it solves: it isolates pattern-matching rules from the shared, stable queueing and redelivery algorithm.
Why needed: a message being published, acknowledged, or dead-lettered are all events a real pub-sub deployment would want to react to (monitoring dashboards, alerting on dead letters).

metadata.alt: DeliveryObserver interface notified by PubSubService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: PubSubService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core routing and redelivery workflow from side effects.
Why needed: message id generation should not be scattered across calling code.

metadata.alt: MessageIdFactory generating sequential M prefixed ids

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: every message is created through one consistent path. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: Message: attributes messageId, topic, payload, deliveryCount; responsibility: represent one published event and its retry history.
Subscriber: attributes subscriberId, topicPatterns, pendingQueue, inFlight, deadLetterList; responsibility: track one consumer's subscriptions and message lifecycle.
PubSubService: the orchestrator; responsibility: route published messages, manage delivery and acknowledgment, and drive redelivery and dead-lettering.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: TopicMatchingStrategy and DeliveryObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: TopicMatchingStrategy: matches(pattern, topic): abstracts away exactly how a subscription pattern compares against a published topic.
DeliveryObserver: onMessagePublished / onMessageAcknowledged / onMessageDeadLettered: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: Three flows below cover a wildcard match delivering a message, a message recovering via redelivery and a late acknowledgment, and a message exhausting its retries into the dead-letter list.

metadata.alt: Publishing to orders.created is routed to a subscriber whose pattern orders.* matches it
An unacknowledged message times out, is redelivered, and is successfully acknowledged on its second delivery
A message that times out a second time exceeds the retry limit and is moved to the dead letter list instead of being redelivered again

blocks.text: The publish-then-acknowledge-or-redeliver workflow, alongside its dead-lettering branch, looks like this:

metadata.alt: A published message is queued per matching subscriber; receiving marks it in flight; acknowledging finishes it, while a timeout without acknowledgment either redelivers it or, past the retry limit, dead letters it

items: Happy path: publish → matching subscribers are enqueued → each receives it → each acknowledges it before any timeout → done.
Recovery path: publish → received but not acknowledged in time → redelivered, delivery count incremented → received again → acknowledged successfully this time.
Failure path: publish → received but never acknowledged, even after redelivery → delivery count exceeds the retry limit → moved to the dead-letter list, no further redelivery attempted.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: subscribe(subscriberId, topicPattern): registers interest in an exact topic or a wildcard pattern.
publish(topic, payload): routes one message copy to every matching subscriber, returning how many subscribers matched.
receive(subscriberId): dequeues the next pending message for a subscriber, marking it in flight.
acknowledge(subscriberId, messageId): confirms successful processing of an in-flight message.
advanceTick() / checkForRedelivery(): advances the deterministic clock and sweeps for timed-out, unacknowledged messages.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: InvalidTopicPatternException: subscribe is called with a blank pattern.
EmptyQueueException: receive is called on a subscriber with nothing currently pending.
InvalidAcknowledgmentException: acknowledge references a message that is not currently in flight for that subscriber.

blocks.text: The critical race is two threads calling receive on the same subscriber at nearly the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing to receive from the same subscriber's queue; synchronization ensures one dequeues the front message before the other reads the queue

blocks.text: Synchronizing the dequeue-and-mark-in-flight step per subscriber ensures two concurrent receive calls can never both walk away with the same message, which would otherwise let it be processed, and separately acknowledged, twice.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A multi-level wildcard or regular-expression matching rule is a new TopicMatchingStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (a monitoring dashboard, a dead-letter alert) is a new DeliveryObserver implementation.
A bounded queue with an overflow policy can be added by checking size in publish before enqueueing.
Unsubscribing can be added as a new method that simply removes a pattern from a subscriber's list, without touching the matching or redelivery logic.
Single Responsibility: Subscriber tracks its own queue and lifecycle, TopicMatchingStrategy decides matching rules, DeliveryObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new matching rules or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to PubSubService.
Liskov Substitution: any TopicMatchingStrategy or DeliveryObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: DeliveryObserver exposes only the three lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: PubSubService depends on the TopicMatchingStrategy and DeliveryObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.
A topic with a different number of segments than a wildcard pattern never matches, even if every corresponding segment up to the shorter length would otherwise agree.
A publish call that matches zero subscribers is not an error, it simply results in no messages being enqueued anywhere.
A subscriber with two different patterns that both match the same published topic still receives exactly one copy of that message, not two.
A message successfully acknowledged is removed from in-flight tracking immediately, so a later, stray redelivery sweep can never act on it.
publish: O(s) where s is the total number of registered subscriptions across every subscriber.
receive / acknowledge: O(1) for the queue and in-flight map operations involved.
checkForRedelivery: O(m) where m is the total number of currently in-flight messages across every subscriber.
Space: O(subscribers + subscriptions + messages in flight and pending) held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: Subscriber, Subscription, Message, and MessageDelivery

items: MESSAGE_DELIVERY tracks the per-subscriber status of one message (pending, in flight, acknowledged, dead lettered) separately from the message itself.
An index on MESSAGE_DELIVERY(subscriberId, status) speeds up finding a subscriber's next pending message.
Add multi-level wildcard support, matching a variable number of trailing segments.
Add a bounded queue per subscriber with a configurable overflow policy.
Support unsubscribing, with a defined policy for already in-flight messages under a removed pattern.
In a distributed deployment, partition topics across multiple broker nodes rather than routing through a single in-process service.

PubSubService, including publish, receive, acknowledge, and the redelivery sweep:

codes.python:
# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class InvalidTopicPatternException(Exception): pass
class EmptyQueueException(Exception): pass
class InvalidAcknowledgmentException(Exception): pass

# The core message routing engine tying every piece together.
class PubSubService:
    def __init__(self, max_retries, timeout_ticks):
        self.subscribers = {}      # subscriberId -> Subscriber
        self.observers = []           # listeners
        self.exact_strategy = ExactTopicMatchingStrategy()      # reused exact matcher
        self.wildcard_strategy = WildcardTopicMatchingStrategy()  # reused wildcard matcher
        self.current_tick = 0                                       # deterministic logical clock
        self.max_retries = max_retries                                 # redelivery attempts allowed before dead lettering
        self.timeout_ticks = timeout_ticks                                # ticks an in-flight message may wait before timing out

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def _subscriber_for(self, subscriber_id):
        if subscriber_id not in self.subscribers:
            self.subscribers[subscriber_id] = Subscriber(subscriber_id)  # create the subscriber on first use
        return self.subscribers[subscriber_id]

    def _strategy_for(self, pattern):
        return self.wildcard_strategy if "*" in pattern else self.exact_strategy  # a wildcard character selects the wildcard strategy

    def subscribe(self, subscriber_id, pattern):
        if pattern is None or pattern.strip() == "":  # blank patterns are not allowed
            raise InvalidTopicPatternException("Topic pattern must not be blank")
        self._subscriber_for(subscriber_id).add_pattern(pattern)  # register the pattern

    def publish(self, topic, payload, factory):
        matched_count = 0  # how many subscribers matched
        for subscriber in self.subscribers.values():  # scan every registered subscriber
            matched = False  # has this subscriber already matched this publish
            for pattern in subscriber.topic_patterns:  # scan every one of their patterns
                if self._strategy_for(pattern).matches(pattern, topic):
                    matched = True
                    break  # one match is enough
            if matched:  # enqueue exactly one copy for this subscriber
                message = Message(factory.next_message_id(), topic, payload)
                subscriber.enqueue(message)
                matched_count += 1
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_message_published(topic, matched_count)  # notify
        return matched_count  # how many subscribers received a copy

    def receive(self, subscriber_id):
        subscriber = self._subscriber_for(subscriber_id)  # the subscriber pulling a message
        if not subscriber.has_pending():  # nothing waiting
            raise EmptyQueueException(f"No pending messages for {subscriber_id}")
        message = subscriber.dequeue_front()  # take the front of the queue
        subscriber.mark_in_flight(message, self.current_tick)  # start tracking it as awaiting acknowledgment
        return message  # hand back the message now in flight

    def acknowledge(self, subscriber_id, message_id):
        subscriber = self._subscriber_for(subscriber_id)  # the subscriber acknowledging
        if not subscriber.is_in_flight(message_id):  # this message is not currently awaiting acknowledgment
            raise InvalidAcknowledgmentException(f"{message_id} is not in flight for {subscriber_id}")
        subscriber.clear_in_flight(message_id)  # done, stop tracking it
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_message_acknowledged(subscriber_id, message_id)  # notify

    def advance_tick(self):
        self.current_tick += 1  # advances the deterministic logical clock by one step

    def check_for_redelivery(self):
        for subscriber in self.subscribers.values():  # scan every subscriber
            timed_out = []  # ids that have timed out this sweep
            for message_id, delivered_at in subscriber.in_flight_delivered_at_tick.items():  # scan every in-flight message
                if self.current_tick-delivered_at >= self.timeout_ticks:
                    timed_out.append(message_id)  # this one has waited too long
            for message_id in timed_out:  # handle each timed out message
                message = subscriber.in_flight_messages[message_id]  # the message itself
                subscriber.clear_in_flight(message_id)  # no longer in flight
                message.increment_delivery_count()  # this counts as a failed attempt
                if message.delivery_count > self.max_retries:  # retries exhausted
                    subscriber.add_to_dead_letter(message)  # set it aside permanently
                    for obs in self.observers:
                        obs.on_message_dead_lettered(subscriber.subscriber_id, message)
                else:  # still has attempts left
                    subscriber.requeue_front(message)  # redeliver it next

items: Why does redelivery put a message back at the FRONT of the queue rather than the back? To preserve as much of the original delivery order as possible, a message that already waited once should generally be retried before newer messages that have not been attempted at all.

Why require the same number of segments for a wildcard match instead of letting a wildcard match zero or more segments? Because a single-segment wildcard is simple to reason about and implement correctly, a multi-level wildcard is explicitly called out as a natural but more complex follow-up.

How would you extend this to guarantee exactly-once delivery instead of at-least-once? Track processed message ids per subscriber (an idempotency-style approach) so a redelivered message that was actually already handled can be recognized and skipped, at the cost of extra bookkeeping.

At-least-once with acknowledgment vs fire-and-forget observer callbacks: acknowledgment-based delivery survives a subscriber that is temporarily slow or crashes mid-processing, at the cost of extra bookkeeping (queues, in-flight tracking, redelivery sweeps) that a simple observer callback does not need.

Single-segment wildcard vs full multi-level wildcard matching: a single-segment wildcard is simple and fast to evaluate, at the cost of not supporting patterns that should match a variable-depth topic hierarchy.

Deterministic tick-based timeouts vs real wall-clock timeouts: tick-based timeouts make behavior fully reproducible and testable, at the cost of needing an explicit driver to advance time, rather than timeouts simply happening on their own in real time.
Persist messages and their per-subscriber delivery status in a durable store using the schema in the Database Design section, so in-flight state survives a service restart.
Replace the deterministic tick counter with a real wall-clock timeout check driven by a background sweep thread in production.
Alert on a growing dead-letter list per subscriber, since it usually signals a bug or outage in that subscriber's processing logic.
Partition topics across multiple broker instances in a large-scale deployment, so publish and delivery load is not bottlenecked on a single process.
